title_en: Air Traffic Control Systems Are Outdated. What’s Being Done to Prevent Another Outage?
excerpt_en: A nationwide flight halt has put the FAA’s aging technology in the spotlight. Upgrades are underway, but preventing future outages will take more than new equipment.

title_en: David Jones’ future looks grim. Is Myer next?
excerpt_en: With Myer’s profitability battered and share price languishing near all-time lows, DJs’ slide into administration raises an uncomfortable question
body_en: When the retailer’s doors slide open, shoppers are greeted by rows of slashed price tags, frantic discounting, and all the other hallmarks of a department store closing down.
Except this isn’t David Jones, the embattled upmarket retailer that is shutting half its 38 stores.
This is its longtime rival, Myer, where entire floors are seemingly permanently on sale.
With Myer’s profitability battered and share price languishing near all-time lows, DJs’ slide into administration raises an uncomfortable question: is Myer next?
‘Sustained erosion of relevance’ At first glance, Myer’s headline numbers seem to defy the retail gloom, with double-digit sales growth to $4.1bn last financial year.

That lift, however, was not driven by surging demand, but by adding sales from the newly acquired apparel chains, Just Jeans, Jay Jays, Portmans, Dotti and Jacqui E, bought from billionaire businessman Solomon Lew’s Premier Investments.

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Meanwhile, to keep registers ringing, Myer employed “higher than planned promotional activity to stimulate demand”, according to its annual report, which reduced its profitability.
The department store has also slashed the value of its brands, down more than $200m in one year alone, in an admission that its labels are worth far less than they once were.

Department stores have faced a “sustained erosion of relevance over the past five years”, according to IBISWorld market researchers, as online platforms win over bargain-hunters and specialists like beauty retailer Mecca prove more nimble in capturing shifting tastes.
DJs and Myer, on the other hand, have been weighed down by long-running physical property leases tied to underperforming stores in their sprawling networks.
Related: David Jones to close half its stores, triggering mass job losses in ‘urgent restructure’
The era of Australian families being fiercely loyal to either David Jones or Myer is long gone, replaced by a grim battle for both chains to stay relevant.

The stress on big department store profitability has been exacerbated by a period of cost of living pressures that have “entrenched deal-hunting behaviour, reshaping how and when consumers engage with department stores”, according to IBISWorld.
Survival tactic or slow-motion bankruptcy Myer, however, has a critical advantage over David Jones: time.
While DJs fell into administration under mounting debts, Myer finished last financial year with a $100m net cash buffer, buying management breathing space to fix the business.

It has been reducing store numbers and with it lease liabilities – down to 56 stores from 60 before the pandemic – which is something David Jones is only doing now that it has collapsed into administration.
For the moment, Myer is leaning into the discounts demanded by shoppers, in the hope that more profitable trading conditions will emerge.
Richard Hemming, the editor at Under The Radar Report, says in retail “volume is everything”.
“If you get the volumes through, that customer base will eventually be in a position to pay more, and when volumes and margins both improve, you get that double effect,” Hemming says.
Related: ‘Very slowly, then all at once’: how David Jones collapsed – podcast

While analysts have mixed views on whether permanent discounting is a smart survival tactic or a slow-motion way to go bankrupt, department stores do need to move huge volumes of stock to keep cash flowing and clear seasonal goods.
They can use those discounts to get more people signed up to their loyalty programs – such as the successful Myer One scheme – in the hope they will become long-term customers.

title_en: SpaceX’s Starship returns to launch pad from orbit in victory for company
excerpt_en: Although booster exploded, company caught upper stage for first time in campaign to make megarocket reusable
body_en: SpaceX’s megarocket Starship returned to its Texas launch tower on Saturday, a milestone in the company’s efforts to make the craft suitable for human spaceflight.
The 171ft (52-meter) bullet-shaped upper stage descended into the clutch of the tower’s mechanical arms, ending a 22hr mission where the craft orbited Earth 14 times.

Starship’s 15th test flight was envisioned as a historic double-catch mission, where all parts of the rocket would be returned intact to the launch site, rather than recovered from the ocean as with some previous test flights.
The hulking spacecraft is composed of two parts: a lower booster stage called Super Heavy, whose Raptor engines powered the orbital ascent, and an upper stage also called Starship.
Those double-catch ambitions were dashed on Friday, when the booster diverted a few minutes after takeoff and exploded in the Gulf of Mexico.
The guidance, navigation and control (GNC) system triggered the no-go.

“It was doing what it was supposed to do. Basically, it detected that the booster was not in the place it was supposed to be to proceed with a catch,” SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said early on Saturday. The booster was also “slightly low on fuel”, according to SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk.
This week’s test flight was still a victory for SpaceX, marking the first time that the company caught its upper stage.
It was also only the second time Starship has entered Earth’s orbit.
The feat comes as the 2028 date nears for Nasa’s plan to return humans to the lunar surface. The agency has contracted SpaceX and Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin for the mission.

“Making more believers by the day,” wrote Nasa administrator Jared Isaacman on X, praising the 15th flight. “One step closer to [the moon].” Isaacman is an ally of Musk, who advised Donald Trump to appoint him to lead Nasa.

SpaceX has plans to ramp up its Starship test flights to a weekly, then twice-weekly cadence, Musk said on a recent earnings call. He has sought to make Starship rapidly reusable so that it can land and take off much like standard airplanes. Musk has touted the rocket’s reusability as a way to reel in the enormous costs of space travel.
Beyond another Moon landing, Musk has also pushed a plan of carrying humans to Mars.
Starship’s advances have also aided the expansion of Musk’s satellite internet empire. The spacecraft deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites during this recent flight.

title_en: I Investigated the Online Sports Betting Industry. DraftKings Shut Down My Account.
excerpt_en: The post I Investigated the Online Sports Betting Industry. DraftKings Shut Down My Account. appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: ProPublica reporter Jake Pearson tests DraftKings’ guardrails at a Manhattan bar this spring. After a ProPublica investigation published this fall, the company closed Pearson’s account. Gerardo del Valle/ProPublica Late last month, I was getting dinner on the table when an email hit my inbox with some bad news.
“Upon review your account has been closed at DraftKings’ discretion,” the message read. “We understand that this is not the decision that you were hoping for but this decision is final.”
I hadn’t bet on sports in months and had withdrawn all but a few cents of my balance. Why, I wondered, would my account even be under review? Was it something I’d said?

In September, I’d published an investigation into how online sports betting companies like DraftKings court customers — and whether the internal guardrails they’ve put in place to stop their users from spiraling out of control are firm enough. For that piece, I’d intentionally bet like a problem gambler, recklessly escalating my betting behavior over 10 weeks. My wagering had been informed by a panel of professional sports bettors, recovering addicts and addiction specialists.
As I flagrantly waved the red flags, DraftKings made me a VIP and assigned me my very own personal host. My recklessness was being rewarded. It just took three weeks and about $6,000 of losses.

What Does Your Data Reveal About Sports Betting Apps? Help ProPublica Find Out. If you’ve bet on sports with FanDuel or DraftKings, you can help ProPublica understand how these apps work. Use our browser extension to download your betting history, then upload your files.

Share Your Experience The company, like the rest of the industry, says it doesn’t want to profit off of addiction, and has invested heavily in a system of tools and in-app prompts designed to help bettors put conditions on their gambling and slow them down. But my experiment raised serious questions about the effectiveness of this system, what’s known as “responsible gaming.”

So on one hand, I could understand how a story like mine, which scrutinized a core business function, might rankle company executives. But on the other hand, DraftKings had been downplaying the significance of my story for weeks.

In an interview for the piece, the company’s chief responsible gaming officer, Lori Kalani, had told me that the system “worked the way it was supposed to” in my case by feeding me some 30 responsible gaming messages over the course of my 10-week betting spree. And on Oct. 22, about a month after publication, DraftKings CEO Jason Robins doubled down, telling a CNBC journalist that he had “personally looked” at my entire betting history and was “pretty proud of how we handled it.” (He also made false claims about my reporting, but I’ve already addressed that on X.)
So as I read the notice of my account closure, I wondered: What changed, exactly?

DraftKings didn’t respond when I asked. All I got was a check in the mail for 94 cents, the remainder of my balance. But what was clear was that my investigation was reaching more and more people — including state regulators and federal lawmakers. Since publication, it had gone viral. A 27-minute, behind-the-scenes documentary of our work that we posted on YouTube on Oct. 10 had been viewed more than 6 million times in just three weeks.
Watch: Inside Our $22K Sports Betting Experiment

Lisa Seville and Nadia Sussman/ProPublica The video offered viewers who may not be familiar with ProPublica (or perhaps not inclined to read 4,000-word stories) a way to learn about the reporting in the venue where so much sports betting content lives. Most of our viewers were young men — the prime sports betting demographic. And boy did they engage, leaving 3,500 comments on YouTube and flooding my inbox with messages about the same features and VIP perks detailed in my story.

Regulators from across the country were citing my investigation when announcing that they were going to take a look for themselves at how DraftKings and its ilk incentivize users to keep betting. Federal and state officials were also demanding answers about how the company lures in its customers and keeps them in the action. In Ohio, regulators were even proposing a rule to restrict the apps’ marketing practices that spoke directly to one of the findings in my piece.
On the morning of Oct. 27, I sent DraftKings a series of questions for a story about that impact.

That evening is when the unsigned notice from DraftKings Support about my account closure appeared in my inbox. Two hours later, the company sent me a formal response to my questions, writing, in part, that “regular conversations and check-ins with regulators are normal course of business” and denying that the company improperly targets losing gamblers.
I may no longer be able to access my account, but I’m still reporting on DraftKings and the online gambling industry.

In fact, right now, we’re collecting wagering data from bettors to better understand how the major operators handle problem gambling. You can help by submitting your data here. If you’ve got a tip, you can also reach me directly at 917-512-0276 and jake.pearson@propublica.org.

title_en: US officials say flight stoppage stemmed from ‘routine maintenance’ as travel chaos continues
excerpt_en: Thousands of flights still canceled as officials blamed ageing air control system for nationwide grounding
body_en: The Trump administration says Friday’s four-hour nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that delayed or canceled thousands of flight stemmed from routine maintenance.

At a news briefing on Saturday, the US transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, said that the issues began when a contractor was performing “routine maintenance” at a remote FAA facility to “switch telecommunications lines” from copper wire to fiber optic cable.
“What we’re working to determine is whether we had incompetence,” Duffy said, “or did they install a faulty router.”
He added: “Once we were able to isolate the work that was being done at this remote location, all of our systems came back online,” and the ground stop was lifted.
However, travel chaos continued across the US on Saturday.
At the briefing, the FAA’s head, Bryan Bedford, apologized to passengers and said he believed that the worst of the disruption “is behind us”.

“We will still have delays and cancellations today, but that will set us up for a full recovery tomorrow,” Bedford said. “Based on everything that we’re hearing from our airline partners, they believe that they’ll be able to have full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday.”

“I want to reiterate: we see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI-related,” he continued. “So we want to be clear that we have a equipment issue, and we’re working through what this defective piece of equipment was.”

Later on Saturday, L3Harris, the federal contractor that Duffy said had been updating air traffic control equipment before the ground stop, released a statement saying that it took the ground stop and its negative effects “on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously”.
The contractor said that it had completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system.
“We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the [Friday] ground stop of our nation’s air travel,” the contractor said.
On Saturday,airlines worked to recover from Friday’s four-hour nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that delayed or canceled thousands of flights.

By of 11am ET on Saturday morning, more than 4,000 flights within, into or out of the US had already been canceled, according to FlightAware, adding to the more than 8,000 cancellations recorded on Friday.

The disruption, which marked the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years, left passengers stranded at airports across the country and facing uncertainty about when they could reach their destinations.
Related: What to know about the rare nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA

Duffy on Friday had blamed the ground stop on an ageing air control system, saying that the communications equipment became “overloaded with data” and was starting to cause inconsistency in the data”.
“Because of that, we shut the system down,” Duffy said.
Duffy on Saturday again mentioned the US having a “decades-old air traffic control system”. “It’s not just old equipment – we have an incredibly old telecommunications system,” he said.
“The work happening was due to the age of the copper wire that we were replacing,” Duffy said on Saturday. “What we’re working determine was whether … it [was] user error or installer error.”
Duffy echoed Bedford in saying “we don’t believe” the disruption resulted from a cyber-attack or some hostile foreign nation.
“This was an FAA system that didn’t meet the moment,” he said. “Our contractor didn’t meet the moment or the equipment didn’t meet the moment and causes the outages.”
Duffy also warned that it would “take us time” to “resume normal operations”.

title_en: I felt nothing but numbness at my dad’s death – but then I read the book he gave me on my wedding day
excerpt_en: Dylan Thomas’s Under Milk Wood reminded me of my dad’s decency and mischief. I laughed as I cried, and realised there’s no right way to go through the grieving process
body_en: I expected to break. But I felt nothing. I did not cry, nor struggle to sleep. I seldom thought of him. I felt only guilt about how little I felt. Ours was a complex relationship. As a teen, I often resented my dad, occasionally despised him. I expected the world and found disappointment. But, as I grew older, I understood that he had struggles of his own. I learned to appreciate his decency and humour, his ability to make everyone laugh with only a few words. I loved my dad, from the first time he held me to the last time I held him.

But still, as weeks turned into months, I struggled to grieve. Then, when my partner and I rearranged our bookshelves, I found the first edition of Under Milk Wood that my parents gave us on our wedding day. I turned the cover and saw the note: “And all the bells of the tills of the town shall ring for our wedding.” It was my mum’s writing, but my dad’s idea. The man loved literature and poetry and considered Dylan Thomas, along with his dad and the Welsh rugby full-back JPR Williams, one of the best men to ever occupy our world.
I cackled as I wept. My grief reminded me of all we’d lost, all we’d been lucky to have

I decided to re-read Under Milk Wood. I took in the first few lines and I suddenly missed him so entirely. My dad grew up in the most northerly village in Wales, on the shore of the Irish Sea, a place full of humour and surrealism. It made him a glutton for wordplay. Names in Under Milk Wood felt all too familiar: Dai Bread, the baker with two wives; Evans the Death, the undertaker; Nogood Boyo, the troublemaker. I heard my dad laugh at the Preacher’s words: “Will you take this woman to be your awful wedded wife?”

Thomas, like my dad, leaned into linguistic excess. Consider the sea, the jollyrodgered sea, dab-filled sea, still still sea, seesaw sea, seas barking like seals, seas green as a bean. I read the play in my old man’s voice, that London-diluted Welsh, with rolling Rs and whispering double Ls. It helped me access grief and mine proved a good grief: I laughed as I cried, cackled as I wept. My grief reminded me of all we’d lost, all we’d been lucky to have.

Small towns and villages possess their own mythology, secured by whispers, spread by gossips, growing wilder by iteration. I remembered my dad, sitting with me in the garden, a laugh so laughable it made me laugh, telling his child stories of his own childhood. A woman in his home town once grew a potato so big they had to build a chip shop round it. There was a crab who people knew on a first-name basis. Sledgehammer-wielding men could not break a boulder, size of a house, until my dad’s taid (grandfather), a stonemason, drew a small cross in white chalk. “Hit here,” he said, walking away. The boulder shattered into a thousand pieces.

Under Milk Wood brought the stories rushing back, with its own chronicles of absurdity. A sea-lawyer from Mumbles dies from blisters. It is always opening time in the never-closing Sailors Arms, because the clock has been stuck on half past 11 for 50-odd years. And Nogood Boyo was a fisher who never caught a fish, but did catch a woman called Mrs Samuels. Stories spread in winding whispers, embellished at every turn. The stories are seemingly implausible. But they are without doubt true, ask anyone.

I realised, spending time in Milk Wood, that there are no roadmaps for grief, nor a right way to grieve. Mine proved tragicomic: pain laced in laughter. And I’m lucky because next month, perhaps next year, I can pick up Under Milk Wood and it’s as if I get to see my old man again. I’ll listen to his stories. I’ll get to hear his voice. So, with that in mind, best to depart on the best part, Eli Jenkins’s prayer, and a stanza that truly captures my dad: We are not wholly bad or good Who live our lives under Milk Wood, And Thou, I know, wilt be the first To see our best side, not our worst.

title_en: Microsoft says services fully restored after global outage hits governments
excerpt_en: Tech company says operations restored to all customers and regions affected by one of worst IT failures in years
body_en: Microsoft has said its service has been fully restored after a massive outage that resulted in widespread disruption to governments, businesses and public services around the world.

The technology company said on Saturday morning it had restored service to the remaining customers affected by one of the worst IT failures in years. On its Microsoft 365 status page, the US-based firm said: “We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions.
“Further updates can be found at MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center.”

The outage, which began on Thursday, affected governments, courts, healthcare services, businesses, airlines and banks. Governments including those of Japan, Singapore and Australia reported that the hours-long episode had affected some of their operations.

In the UK, where NHS England has a five-year deal to use Microsoft 365, vital public services were hit, with hospital staff resorting to paper records and one union reporting that ambulance services had suffered a “serious impact”.

The already backlogged court system was also hit, with juries in some cases being sent home early or prisoners not being sent to court, while at Minshull Street crown court in Manchester staff scrambled to locate a fax machine.

In the US, school districts told parents they must reach out by phone or online apps to contact their child’s school, while staffers at the House of Representatives told Politico they had lost a day of work.
One detention facility in Colorado said they were unable to take online bond payments to release detainees and told anyone needing to post bond for immediate release to do so in person at the jail.

In Australia, many people who rely on Microsoft 365 reported being unable to access their inboxes, including at councils, courts and schools. The federal police and Asio, Australia’s national domestic security and intelligence agency, were also affected by the outage.
Asio’s director general, Mike Burgess, said the agency’s systems “operate on multiple levels”, adding that they had been affected “on one level, yes, but not completely”.
Across Europe, government agencies in the Netherlands, Belgium and France reported problems, with a French municipality instructing citizens to use the phone instead of emailing.

In Japan, government email services became unavailable and staff resorted to text messaging. The shipping firm Sagawa Express was unable to accept some online reservations while Taisho, a major pharmaceutical company, said it was having to handle orders by phone.

The Indian airlines IndiGo and Akasa Air said their email support services were affected, and Taiwanese security firms, life insurers and investment trust companies told Reuters that fund management services had been disrupted.

Users reported that Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and the AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Downdetector, an online tracker, said it received outage reports from users in more than 70 countries and territories.
About 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft said on its website. Problems began at about midday on Thursday in the US and at 6pm in the UK.

The Washington-based company apologised on Friday for the disruptions and said the outage was “not related to cyber” or artificial intelligence agents. It said the incident “was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced” after a recent network change.

The disruptions offer the latest example of the cascading problems that can erupt when multiple communications and technology platforms depend on the same provider. The outage has fuelled concerns in the UK about an overreliance on a small number of tech companies.

Steven Murdoch, a professor of security engineering at University College London, told the Guardian an outage of this size was usually “the result of some surprising interaction between systems. Each of the systems is normally quite well understood but interactions between them are complex and frequently the cause of large outages like this.
“It’s very hard to build a complex system without there being some risk of some failure.”

Tim Clement-Jones, a former chair of the House of Lords artificial intelligence select committee, said the widespread outages of vital government services were an “I-told-you-so moment” highlighting Britain’s dependence on US tech.

Jeremy Singer, a professor at the University of Glasgow’s School of Computing Science, said: “This problem serves to emphasise the dependence we have built on one company’s digital infrastructure, and may lead us to question whether we need more resilience in our IT ecosystem.”
The total number of people affected was not clear, but Microsoft said in January it had more than 450m paid commercial subscriptions to its 365 services.

title_en: Greenpeace boulders may delay building of £12bn windfarms in North Sea
excerpt_en: Activists dumped rocks off Norfolk coast on site of Burnham-backed project in protest against seabed trawling
body_en: The giant offshore windfarms backed by Andy Burnham this week may face unexpected stumbling blocks after Greenpeace activists unwittingly dumped about 15 tonnes of boulders on to the site as part of a campaign against seabed trawling in the North Sea.

Greenpeace created the “boulder barrier” to safeguard harbour porpoises off the Norfolk coast by dropping giant stone blocks, each weighing up to 2 tonnes, on to the sea floor to prevent a method of fishing known as bottom trawling.

The barrier will pose an additional challenge for the green energy developers because most of the boulders were dropped on to the site earmarked for one of the UK’s biggest planned windfarms, known as the Norfolk Vanguard project.

Greenpeace began dumping boulders on to the site, without consent from the marine authority, days before the prime minister told the Cop31 summit that the UK would invest £1bn of public money in the Vanguard West and Vanguard East windfarms in what is believed to be the biggest investment of its kind in UK history.
The Guardian understands that Greenpeace checked the seabed for any existing cables, pipelines or shipwrecks, but it was not aware of the plans to build the Vanguard East windfarm.

Interactive The creation of the underwater barrier in one of “the most heavily trawled” areas of the southern North Sea was timed to coincide with the premiere of the BBC’s Blue Planet III documentary, narrated by Sir David Attenborough.
Some boulders bear the signatures of celebrities including Simon Pegg and Benedict Cumberbatch, who have voiced marine conservation documentaries, and agreed to support the Greenpeace campaign.

However, they are likely to be removed within months after renewable energy developers agreed a £12bn deal alongside the UK government to begin building the offshore windfarm next year. Industrial fishing activities, including bottom trawling, are also likely to move elsewhere to avoid the construction area.

The Guardian understands that the offshore wind developer, the German utility company RWE, is in talks with Greenpeace to verify the exact placement of the boulders so that they can update the seabed surveys they began last summer. The company is also investigating any potential impact to the construction of the project or its undersea cables.

A spokesperson for RWE described its communication with Greenpeace as “constructive” and said the company would “continue to investigate the precise implications” for the Norfolk Vanguard East project.
Will McCallum, the co-executive director of Greenpeace UK, said any suggestion that the boulders would cause a genuine obstacle was “absurd”.
“Anyone familiar with offshore wind in the North Sea knows that energy companies routinely move naturally occurring boulders from the seabed before building windfarms,” he said.
“Some of these boulders can be 10 times heavier than those we placed.

“Greenpeace has long championed offshore wind and will continue to do so. While we wait for this windfarm to be built, our boulders will provide an essential barrier to destructive bottom trawlers that are decimating the seabed in this protected area.”

title_en: How Trump’s War on Offshore Wind Upended a “Limitless” Future for Thousands of New England Workers
excerpt_en: The post How Trump’s War on Offshore Wind Upended a “Limitless” Future for Thousands of New England Workers appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: The Vineyard Wind farm off the coast of Massachusetts in May Eleonora Bianchi/The New Bedford Light On a hot July day in 2022, then-President Joe Biden gave a speech from the ruins of a coal-fired power plant on the southern coast of Massachusetts.
Standing where ships once delivered coal for combustion, he said the same dock would soon launch components for wind power out to sea.

He praised an Italian company’s plans to build a new factory there, set to create 250 jobs and supply American-made undersea power cables to what was then a line of offshore wind projects waiting to be built along the coast.
Four years later, weeds and tall grass have reclaimed the dirt lot on which Biden spoke.

Ben Berke/Ocean State Media Eleonora Bianchi/The New Bedford Light Then-President Joe Biden gave a speech at Brayton Point in Somerset, Massachusetts, in 2022. Four years later, the promised factory has been canceled. Prysmian Caleb Kenna for ProPublica An architectural rendering of plans for an offshore wind cable factory on Brayton Point, compared with a 2026 photograph of the same area. A 20-minute drive east, in New Bedford, hundreds of workers who helped assemble wind turbine parts from Canada and Europe over the last three years have given way to seagulls and geese. The birds shuffle along the now-empty pier the state of Massachusetts spent $140 million to build for offshore wind development.
In nearby Providence, Rhode Island, a newly built factory that manufactured offshore wind turbine foundation platforms has emptied out.

Ben Berke/Ocean State Media Eleonora Bianchi/The New Bedford Light Union members worked for three years assembling turbines on New Bedford’s waterfront. The wind developer that planned to use the port facility next has instead delayed its project indefinitely. Amid the Trump administration’s multifront war against offshore wind, the cost on the ground in New England, the launchpad of the country’s offshore wind industry, can be seen in empty warehouses, silent marine terminals and ledgers recording hundreds of millions of dollars of state investment that may not be recouped.
ProPublica partnered with Ocean State Media, The Connecticut Mirror and the New Bedford Light to document the consequences of the administration’s efforts.

James Estrin/The New York Times/Redux Eleonora Bianchi/The New Bedford Light A factory that made turbine components on Providence’s waterfront is now sitting empty. Many offshore wind projects faced a precarious future before President Donald Trump retook office. Rising construction costs driven by inflation and supply chain shortages forced some developers to back out of contracts to build wind farms and supply electricity to states. Various groups have also fought construction of projects saying they disrupt marine ecosystems and mar coastal views.

But last year, the administration temporarily forced five projects to stop construction, further clouding the horizon. Courts allowed the developers to proceed, but that has not eliminated the threat. Last month, the U.S. Department of the Interior asked a court for permission to reconsider a key permit for one of those five projects, Revolution Wind, which is already up and running and can power more than 350,000 New England homes at maximum capacity.

The administration also has frozen future development on all offshore wind farms, including a cluster of projects that haven’t been built but proposed to power up to 1.7 million New England homes. It has blocked or is seeking review of the permits that would allow these to be built. Meanwhile, the administration is paying other wind developers billions of dollars to sell back their leases and walk away.

At a press conference Monday, Trump said he supports a bipartisan bill that would accelerate U.S. energy development. When a reporter pointed out that the bill includes wind energy, Trump said he would not approve “wind turbines ’cause wind turbines are a major loser.”
The upheaval has had ripple effects. The cable company Biden touted decided not to build its factory, citing “long-term trends in the U.S. market.”
Port cities like New Bedford, Massachusetts, and New London, Connecticut, are left trying to hold onto the economic gains they have made building wind farms.
Read More About On-the-Ground Impacts From Our Partners The Connecticut Mirror: Offshore wind offered a ‘limitless’ future for Connecticut. Trump scuttled the plan.
The New Bedford Light: Fishermen’s offshore wind work drying up
Ocean State Media: Offshore wind saved a struggling New Bedford union. Now its future is uncertain.

As recently as last winter, New Bedford, a historic whaling and textile manufacturing center, had hotels, offices and piers buzzing with offshore wind workers. Local businesses from caterers to cleaners to fuel suppliers landed new contracts servicing the wind industry.

In New London — another port once central to the whaling industry — officials worked with one of the world’s largest wind developers to pump more than $300 million of public and private funds into a state-owned pier. Despite significant cost overruns and some early construction challenges, the effort transformed the pier into a staging area for the wind industry.

Wind turbine components are stored at the State Pier in New London, waiting to be loaded onto installation vessels en route to Danish wind developer Ørsted’s offshore wind farms. The last of three consecutive projects is expected to be completed next year, but no others are fully permitted. Sarah Gordon/The Connecticut Mirror Over the last four years, the pier has been a hive of activity. Hundreds of workers were employed loading and offloading turbine parts — with blades the length of a football field — from specially designed ships, some with names drawn from Greek mythology. Local companies also found work supporting the industry, including one that offered water rescue training for people working on construction sites offshore.

title_en: The SS United States has been deliberately sunk – this is how marine life will colonise the world’s largest artificial reef
excerpt_en: A month by month guide, by a marine ecologist and keen scuba diver.
body_en: As a marine ecologist and keen scuba diver, I’ve long been fascinated by what happens when a large structure is introduced to the sea. Within hours, microscopic organisms begin colonising its surfaces, forming a thin biological layer. Over the following months and years, barnacles, mussels, sponges and other marine life become established, creating a new habitat that attracts fish and a diverse range of species.

This week, one of the world’s most famous ocean liners, the SS United States, was sunk off the coast of Florida. At 302 metres long, it has become the world’s largest artificial reef. It is a very exciting prospect to one day dive on such a giant, and to see how it changes as marine life makes it home.

The SS United States was built as a luxury ocean liner, and its maiden voyage in 1952 captured the coveted Blue Riband by crossing the Atlantic in only three days and ten hours – a passenger liner record that remains unbroken.

As the years went by, commercial jetliners superseded transatlantic sea travel, and the vessel was retired and neglected for decades. Rather than facing the ignominy of a breaker’s yard, the legendary ship was bought by Okaloosa County, Florida, to turn it into a diving attraction.

The SS United States is a particularly enormous structure to introduce to the seabed – longer even than the Titanic. It will rest in around 55 metres of water, with its upper sections rising to within about 17 metres of the surface. This will create habitats at different depths, making it an unusually varied site for both wildlife and divers of different abilities.
It will also eclipse the nearby 275-metre aircraft carrier USS Oriskany, deliberately sunk in 2006, to become the largest artificial reef on Earth.
So what do we expect to happen? Here’s a suggested ecological succession pattern, month-by-month.

First, microorganisms arrive The first organisms to colonise the SS United States will be almost invisible. Within hours of immersion, marine bacteria and microalgae will begin attaching themselves to its cleaned metal surfaces, forming a thin layer of “biofilm”.

This slime is the foundation of the new ecosystem. As the biofilm develops, it releases chemical cues that help drifting larvae recognise the surface as a suitable place to settle. Carried by Gulf currents, these tiny organisms begin attaching themselves to the structure. By the end of the first three months, a variety of small animals and algae will have established themselves on the hull, beginning the transformation of bare metal into a living reef.

Then the ship becomes covered in marine life As the biofilm matures, larger organisms arrive to feed on it. These include more mobile invertebrates like sea urchins and porcelain crabs, and filter-feeders like oysters and mussels which attach themselves to vertical walls where the currents tend to send the most nutrients their way.

This shipwreck has attracted coral, fish – and a hawksbill turtle. Muh ridzwan / shutterstock Fish and larger predators move in By the end of the first year, hard corals will begin to establish themselves permanently. The transformation will still be in its early stages, but over the next five to ten years the hull will become increasingly encrusted with corals, sponges and other marine life. At some point, casual divers will no longer see a ship covered in coral, but a coral-covered reef that happens to contain a ship.
As the reef develops, fish will be attracted by the shelter and the growing supply of food. Smaller fish will begin to find refuge to evade open-water predators.

Snappers and groupers are among the medium-sized reef fish that will begin to take up permanent residency around the wreck, using the long internal corridors for protection. Larger predators, including barracuda, king mackerel and sharks, could also patrol its decks and upper sections.

The ship’s enormous size and varied structure will offer a range of habitats, from sheltered spaces for smaller fish to exposed areas where larger, free-swimming species can hunt. Over time, these interactions could create a complex food web, turning the wreck into a significant biological hotspot.

A common misconception is that artificial reefs simply concentrate fish that were already present, leaving surrounding waters poorer. In reality, while some fish are attracted from elsewhere, a large reef structure also creates vast amounts of new habitat and food.

As corals, sponges, barnacles and other reef builders colonise the wreck, they create food and shelter that did not previously exist, allowing the ecosystem to support more life overall. The result is generally not an underwater crowd gathered around a ship, but a gradual increase in the total amount of marine life the area can support.

Another widespread misconception is that marine scientists “seed” artificial reefs with organisms or their larvae. In reality, colonisation happens naturally: the Gulf of Mexico already harbours an abundant pool of drifting larvae and migratory fish. Artificially introducing marine life is unnecessary and risks introducing non-native species or pathogens.

Instead, human engineering is largely about preparing the ship for sinking. This includes removing hazards such as oil, asbestos and loose wires, and sealing off parts of the vessel to prevent divers getting disorientated or lost in silt-outs deep in the hull.

The scuttling of the SS United States represents a rare convergence of maritime history, ecology, and engineering. Transformed into the world’s largest artificial reef, this record-breaking ocean liner could potentially anchor a vibrant marine ecosystem for decades to come. I’m looking forward to seeing how that transformation unfolds – and maybe, one day, exploring it myself.

title_en: How groomers operate – and why victims become trapped
excerpt_en: The claims against David Walliams have raised some familiar tropes.
body_en: nikkimeel/Shutterstock Entertainer and children’s author David Walliams is alleged to have used his fame to approach teenage girls, in some cases reportedly initiating sexual contact with them. Walliams has denied the allegations, but the claims raise some familiar tropes about grooming: why did she go, why didn’t she say no, why didn’t she tell anyone?
After a legal battle, ITV News and The Guardian have now published the findings of a three-year investigation into Walliams, reporting allegations that date back to 2003.

In this and other cases, there will always be people who focus not on the claims, but on the young person and what they should have done differently. Linguistic research on how grooming actually works suggests that this instinct is exactly the result that grooming is designed to produce.

Many people imagine sexual grooming as a recognisable and clearly staged process. Build friendship, then trust, then secrecy – all leading towards the offender’s ultimate goal of sexual gratification. But if this were the case, victims could notice the steps and walk away.

Along with a colleague, I undertook linguistic analysis of real chatroom conversations between convicted offenders and adult volunteers posing as 12 to 14-year-old girls. The conversations were made public by the now defunct organisation Perverted Justice, whose activity led to the apprehension and conviction of the offenders. In our analysis, we did not find the pattern mentioned above.

We identified 14 recurring “moves” – parts of the offenders’ language that have particular functions. These include building rapport (for instance by sharing personal stories), assessing risk by checking parents’ schedules or the presence of a boyfriend, escalating sexual topics and planning offline meetings. But these moves overlapped and repeated, with no typical structure emerging.
Rather, offenders seemed to tailor their grooming styles, perhaps according to their individual goals and who they believed they were talking to.

Trust and rapport What was consistent was the large amount of rapport-building, which often ran through the whole interaction. Grooming research invariably shows that rapport-building and trust development are the central devices used to persuade and manipulate.

This may be through compliments, sharing personal information and declarations of trust. Grooming strategies are designed to develop intimacy and trust, isolate the victim and dismantle the “red flags” that might alert them to the manipulative nature of the conversation. Trust development makes it much harder for victims to notice devious intentions – there is no obvious point at which the young person has failed to spot something plainly visible.

Offenders in our data spent much of their conversations sizing up their targets. They would try to work out whether a target was likely to engage, suited their preferences, was accessible and unlikely to expose them. We called this a “risk-reward ratio assessment” – in other words, a judgement about whether this person was worth their effort.

In another study, we examined the case of an offender who took a scattergun approach, in this case targeting nearly 1,000 potential young victims. This individual would strategically cycle through an array of fake online personas to identify the one most likely to “hook” his target. The vast majority ignored or rejected his first advance, at which point they were dropped. But this is the point of the scattergun approach; a small percentage, usually the most vulnerable, will respond.
Our work also revealed how offenders manage the risk of being caught. For many we studied, a key strategy was to use language that shifted responsibility on to the target.

Questions were often formulated to elicit sexually explicit content by positioning the target as the one in control. The groomer might say, for example, “how far do you want to go”, “tell me what you wanna do”. This phrasing both presumes interest and makes declining more difficult, while laying the groundwork to say later that the young person had led the conversation.

Another feature was what we termed the “mitigating lol”. This could be something like “u should send me a nude vid lol”. This served to reduce the impact of a sexual question by implying playfulness. It also supports future claims that the requests was insincere – possibly a useful tactic in a trial. We can only infer the purpose, but it points to the same strategy of building in deniability.

I cannot speak directly to the Walliams allegations, but when it comes to celebrities in general, the task of building trust and rapport may well be easier. The victims already feel they know them, and are made to feel special by being approached. It’s also easy to see how the perks of celebrity could do much of the persuasive work.

A widely used definition of grooming across linguistics and psychology describes preparing the child, their significant adults and the wider environment for abuse. Compliance and secrecy are explicit goals. They are not evidence of the victim’s character.

So when people ask, “why did they keep replying?” or “why did they go to the house?” they are asking why a technique that was designed to engage did in fact keep them engaged. When we ask, “why didn’t they tell anyone?” we are questioning why a strategy engineered to cultivate silence did exactly that.

Grooming involves a complex network of strategies. But we know it is never the young person’s behaviour that’s the problem. The “perfect victim” who resists every advance and raises the alarm at every opportunity is a myth.

title_en: The uncomfortable question at the heart of Europe’s identity crisis
excerpt_en: Across Europe, parts of the radical right are increasingly trying to fuse ethnicity and culture into a new definition of national belonging.
body_en: What makes someone French, German, British or Danish? Is it the passport they hold, the language they speak, or the ancestry they inherit?

Across Europe, parts of the nationalist right are increasingly blurring the distinction between culture and ethnicity. The result is a view of national identity where belonging depends on where a person’s ancestors come from.
This way of thinking is called ethnonationalism – where membership of a nation depends on ethnic background or ancestry, rather than simply on citizenship or cultural identity.

In Denmark, where I live, this idea has recently taken a striking turn. A few months ago, I appeared in a televised debate opposite a former political adviser to a Danish right-wing party who, in essence and quite seriously, argued that to be Danish, you have to be able to tolerate milk.

The argument draws on the fact that the ability to digest lactose, the sugar in milk, is more common among people with Northern European ancestry. The suggestion was that this biological trait could help define who is truly Danish.

Others on the nationalist right soon made similar arguments. One commentator wrote that Danish ancestry should be the basis for defining Danishness, because cultural “spirit” ultimately derives from blood.
But while the ability to digest milk might seem an absurd test of Danishness, the underlying question is a serious one and it extends far beyond Denmark.

When citizenship isn’t enough Similar ideas are gaining ground elsewhere in Europe. In France, Marine Le Pen’s nationalist political project has promoted an ethnonationalist view of national identity, in which ancestry plays a central role in defining who belongs.

While Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has also made ethnonationalist claims as it has gained ground. In 2025, Germany’s domestic intelligence agency classified the party as right-wing extremist, although the legal status and implications of that classification have been contested.

These movements differ, but they raise a common question: can someone be a citizen of a country, live there for years and participate in its society, yet still be considered an outsider because of their ancestry?
This distinction between legal citizenship and supposedly authentic national belonging is central to the nationalist right’s calls for “remigration” across Europe.

The term is used by proponents to argue that people with migrant backgrounds should be removed from countries where they live, even when they have citizenship or were born there. This can include calling for the mass deportation of people deemed not to belong to the nation because of their ethnicity, ancestry or cultural background.

Such ideas often overlap with the so-called “great replacement” conspiracy theory, which claims those with non-Western backgrounds are replacing existing populations. And elements of this narrative have been adopted by nationalist and far-right politicians across Europe.

Something has changed The word “ethnocultural” brings together two ideas: that a nation has a distinctive culture and that this culture belongs to a particular ethnic group. It suggests that national identity is not simply something people can learn or participate in, but something rooted in their origins.

Some researchers describe the shift in how nationalist politicians talk about national identity as a “ cultural turn ”. Rather than focusing explicitly on race or ancestry, they increasingly talk about protecting a country’s culture, values and way of life.

On the surface, that might sound more inclusive; people can learn the language or adopt new customs. But if a country’s culture is treated as something you inherit from your ancestors, rather than something you can share and take part in, the boundary between insiders and outsiders remains.

European values? My research in Denmark has examined how national identity has changed over time. The findings suggest that, despite what some nationalist political groups argue, most people do not see ancestry as the defining feature of national belonging.

The Danish Values Study, part of a wider European survey, asks people about their beliefs and values. Comparing responses from the most recent 2008 and 2017 surveys, the proportion who thought being Danish was mainly about having Danish roots fell from 19% to 15%.

Meanwhile, around four in five saw being Danish as a matter of belonging to the country and its society rather than having a particular ethnic background. This figure remained almost unchanged, at 77% in 2008 and 79% in 2017. These findings offer a different perspective from the idea that national identity is rooted in blood (or milk).

This understanding also has roots in history. The Danish theologian NFS Grundtvig expressed a vision of national belonging in his 1848 poem Folkeligheden: “To a people all belong, who count themselves as part of it”. In other words, belonging is something people can claim for themselves, rather than something dictated by family background.

That said, the poem has featured in debates about Danish identity, with figures on the right using it to argue for a narrower definition of national belonging, while others see it as an argument for a more inclusive idea of Danishness.

And ultimately this raises the broader question: who has the legitimacy to define who belongs to a country or not? A question that will likely be a defining feature of European politics for years to come.
